title: Jacob Wrestles at Peniel
summary: The night before Jacob meets Esau again, a mysterious figure wrestles with him until daybreak. Jacob leaves with a blessing, a new name—Israel—and a lasting limp. He names the place Peniel because, as he says, he has seen God face to face and survived. The encounter does not remove his fear or explain the wrestler's identity, but Jacob limps onward to meet Esau, who embraces him.
historical_context: Genesis places the struggle at the Jabbok crossing during Jacob's return to Canaan after years away from Esau. Jacob has sent his family and possessions across the river and is left alone before the encounter. At dawn the struggle ends; in the next scene Jacob sees Esau approaching with his household. This setting ties the night scene to the unresolved family conflict rather than presenting it as an isolated tale. The narrative supplies the location and sequence, not an independently dated historical account.
canonical_context: The name Israel becomes the name of Jacob's descendants, making this personal encounter part of the Bible's account of Israel's beginnings. Hosea 12 returns to Jacob's struggle and describes him as seeking God's favor, showing how the prophet rereads the ancestral story for a later audience. Hosea's interpretation adds a perspective without supplying the name that Genesis leaves unrevealed.
literary_context: The scene interrupts Jacob's preparations to meet Esau. It begins with Jacob alone at night, delays resolution through a struggle that lasts until dawn, and ends with a new name and an injury. Jacob calls the place Peniel, but the figure refuses to give his own name, leaving the encounter deliberately mysterious. The next scene shifts from this fearful night to Esau's unexpected embrace, so Jacob's altered walk and new name accompany him into the reunion.
covenantal_significance: Jacob receives a blessing and the name Israel, linking one ancestor's encounter to the identity of the people who bear that name. Genesis presents the struggle as both a wound and a blessing, and leaves the opponent unnamed; Jacob interprets the encounter as seeing God and surviving. Hosea later reflects on Jacob's struggle as seeking God's favor. Keeping those passages distinct preserves the mystery of Genesis while showing how a later prophet drew meaning from it.
canonical_role: Explains Israel's name and frames the people as marked by struggle, dependence, and blessing.
